newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA LEU DIPS, DOWNSWING TO CONTINUE-TRADERS.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA LEU DIPS, DOWNSWING TO CONTINUE-TRADERS.

text.p: Romania's leu currency lost some nine percent at this week's open, and traders expect it to fall further on a hard currency-squeezed interbank market.
The leu slipped to 4,700/800 to the dollar on Monday, and traders expect it to slide below 5,000 this week: "I see the leu closing the week at 5,200/300" one dealer said.
"This looks to be the level at which energy prices will be adjusted," he added.

But operators ruled out a sharper slump in the coming days, despite scarce dollar supplies as Romania is caught in a classic trade squeeze with hard currency earnings trickling in from exports and import demand high.

The new reformist government, in power since the defeat of ex-communists in last November's elections, doubled petrol prices starting January, aligning them to world levels, as suggested by the International Monetary Fund.
Bucharest has yet to act on pledges to liberalise the foreign exchange market -- now restricted to only four dealer banks -- a priority for resuming loan talks with the Fund.

Talks on a new IMF deal are due to start next week. The Fund suspended a three-year stand-by loan worth $460 million last year over foreign exchange curbs and overspending by the former leftist administration.

The leu's downward move began to gather pace after the new cabinet took office last December. So far the central bank, whose hard currency reserves were $855.2 million at end-1996, has refrained from intervening to halt the leu's downswing.
The interbank leu sank about 15 percent to the greenback from end-1996, but the gap between interbank rates and retail prices did not narrow, amid inflationary expectations.
At Bucharest currency shops the dollar has breached the 6,000 threshold, gaining some nine percent from January 1.
Prices closer to retail levels could be obtained on the interbank market, where cross trading in other currencies, like the German mark or French franc, yield weaker leu-dollar rates.
"The recent price hikes have also undermined confidence in the leu and banks have yet to respond by raising their rates after tightened monetary policies," one trader said.
Electricity and heating prices are also expected to go up this week, with economists predicting a quickening of inflation to over 10 percent this month.
Year-on-year inflation stood at 47.4 percent last November, well above a 20 percent target agreed with the IMF.

In a bid to calm down soaring inflation the central bank (BNR) jacked up the discount rate to 50 percent from 35 percent starting January. Its auctioned credit rate jumped last week to 59.23 from 53 percent.
